passages.title: Reading Comprehension I – Multicultural Toronto
passages.instructions: Read the following text, and answer the questions that follow. For items 1–6, choose the most appropriate answer according to the information in the text. For items 7–10, choose the best contextual meaning for each highlighted word or phrase in the text.
paragraphs: Since 1971 Canada has had a policy to encourage multiculturalism, and Canadians like to say their society is a mosaic, not a melting pot. The Italians got off the streetcar in one neighbourhood, Vietnamese nearby, Chinese a few stops east. Each community is intact, a piece in the mosaic, each seeking a place in the national design. The perennial question in multicultural Toronto, is whether there is, in fact, any design.

I got off at Chinatown stop, where the merchants sell shark cartilage, fresh taro root, and tall bundles of raw sugarcane on the sidewalks. Toronto’s underlying orderliness was evident even here, amid the hectic buying and selling. The sidewalk stands all stay carefully within yellow painted lines marking the spaces where the shopkeepers are allowed to do business.

Ko, an entrepreneur who came to Toronto from Hong Kong in 1967, showed me the neighbourhood. “Hong Kong is very busy,” he said. “You have to walk very fast, talk very fast, work very fast, eat very fast, and time goes very fast. There’s not much life in Toronto. People from Hong Kong don’t like that. But they settle in Toronto because they want the better education, the low crime.”
“Are you a Canadian?” I asked.
“I am a Canadian citizen,” he replied.
“But in here?” I said, indicating his heart.
“My kids are Canadian. They eat at McDonald’s. They like french fries, not rice.”
“What does being Canadian mean to you?” I asked.
But the subject of being Canadian made Ko move quickly from one point to another: He didn’t know what it meant to be Canadian, except that it was like being American. Only safer.

It occurred to me that Toronto has remained law-abiding partly because so many newcomers, arriving from places like Vietnam in the 1970s and ‘80s, have seen how bad the world can get when order slips away into madness.
passages.note: Text as printed. The highlighted (bold) words in the paper are: intact, hectic, entrepreneur, slips away.

passages.title: Reading Comprehension II – Tackling economic inequality
passages.instructions: Read the following text, and answer the questions that follow. For items 66–75, choose the most appropriate answer according to the information in the text. For items 76–80, choose the best contextual meaning for each highlighted word in the text.
paragraphs: As growth slows in many economies of the developed world, economic inequality has reached new heights. The main reasons for the rise in inequality is the explosion in gains by those at the very top of the income distribution. But the circumstances of those at the bottom have contributed, too. Poverty rate in the developed world stands some percentage points higher than it did decades earlier. The good news is that present levels of inequality are not inevitable. There are concrete steps governments can take to tackle inequality.

Economists have described a race between education, which increases the supply of skilled workers, and technological change, which increases the demand for them. Since demand has grown faster than supply, the premium paid to skilled workers has increased, widening the wage differential between the skilled and the unskilled worker. One of the policy advices, therefore, is for societies to invest more in education and training.

Most technological advancements are the product of decisions made by research managers, businesspeople, investors, governments, and consumers. These decisions affect the degree to which technological change favours skilled or unskilled workers and, more generally, the degree to which it favours capital over labour. A company may, for example, decide to invest in robotizing its production which would reduce the demand for labour. Governments should take an active interest in the direction of technological change by considering employment and other social needs when allocating public research funds. It might make sense, for instance, to shift priorities from driverless cars, which will likely reduce jobs, to technology that helps the elderly stay in their homes (rather than in care centres), which would increase the demand for caregivers.

The story about inequality is also incomplete in that it focuses on individual earnings – the gap between pay at the top and pay at the bottom. It ignores taxes and social transfers, which play a large role in determining how much income a household receives. To help the redistribution of income, the first requirement is to make income taxes more progressive, i.e., the more income one has the more taxes one pays. The top tax marginal rate should rise from 45 percent to 65 percent – closer to the rates that prevailed for much of the twentieth century.

Governments should also reform the way they tax the transfer of wealth, such as inheritance. All wealth received over one’s lifetime in the form of inheritance and gifts should be subject to taxes. Those who gave away their wealth broadly, i.e., to many recipients, rather than concentrating it on one recipient should be rewarded. The revenues collected from such wealth-transfer tax should be used to fund a minimum inheritance for everyone in the country on reaching the age of 18. Such egalitarianism would promote equality of opportunity.

Reducing income inequality is not just about taxes and wealth transfers; governments also need to tackle unemployment. Governments should establish an explicit target for unemployment, such as a minimum acceptable rate of unemployment, just as many governments do with inflation. Moreover, governments can be asked to promote maximum employment. The government can also act as an employer of last resort by offering guaranteed jobs. Jobs are only part of the story, since many people who work remain poor – hence the need to raise the minimum wage.
passages.note: Text as printed (‘The main reasons … is’, ‘policy advices’ are slips in the original). Highlighted (bold) words: explosion, race, allocating, determining, egalitarianism.

questions.stem: The purpose of the writer is to show how Canada’s immigration policy has affected
explanation_steps: The passage starts with Canada’s multicultural policy and then describes only Toronto: its neighbourhoods, Chinatown, a Hong Kong immigrant and Toronto’s orderliness.
America is mentioned only in a comparison, Hong Kong only as the place Ko came from, and native Canadians not at all. Answer: B.
tips: A purpose question is about the WHOLE text – pick the option that the passage keeps returning to.

similar_questions.stem: A passage describes how a new dam changed farming, fishing and daily life in one river valley. The writer’s purpose is to show how the dam affected
explanation_steps: All the examples come from the valley. Answer: B.

questions.stem: According to the information in the passage, one of the following is true about Hong Kong and Toronto.

options.A: Life in Hong Kong is faster than life in Toronto.
options.B: Hong Kong is richer than Toronto.
options.C: Hong Kong is safer than Toronto.
options.D: Hong Kong is more friendly than Toronto.

explanation_steps: Ko: “Hong Kong is very busy … You have to walk very fast, talk very fast … There’s not much life in Toronto.”
So life in Hong Kong is faster. Wealth and friendliness are not mentioned; safety favours Toronto (‘the low crime’). Answer: A.
tips: Reject options that add information the text never gives (richer, more friendly).

similar_questions.stem: ‘In the village everybody greets you; in the city nobody has time to stop.’ Which is true?
explanation_steps: Greeting everyone = friendliness in the village. Answer: B.

questions.stem: People come from Hong Kong to Toronto to settle because

options.C: Toronto is safer than Hong Kong.

explanation_steps: Ko: “they settle in Toronto because they want the better education, the low crime.”
Better education = A; low crime = safer = C. Crowding is not given as a reason. Answer: E (A and C).
tips: With ‘A and B / A and C’ options, check each letter separately against the text.

similar_questions.stem: ‘Many students choose this college for its low fees and its excellent library.’ Why do students choose it?
explanation_steps: Both low fees (A) and the library (B) are stated. Answer: D.

questions.stem: The writer asked a character in the story, ‘Are you Canadian?’ The character replied to the question by saying:

options.B: He is a citizen of Hong Kong.
options.D: He did not give a clear answer.

explanation_steps: The direct reply to “Are you a Canadian?” was: “I am a Canadian citizen,” he replied.
‘My kids are Canadian’ (C) answers the NEXT question (“But in here?”), and his vagueness (D) concerns ‘What does being Canadian mean to you?’. Answer: A.
tips: Match the exact question in the stem to the line that answers it – neighbouring lines are traps.

similar_questions.stem: “Do you like Asmara?” I asked. “It is a beautiful city,” she said. “But would you live here?” “My brother lives here.” What was her reply to the first question?
explanation_steps: The first question is answered by ‘It is a beautiful city’. Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following represents a message the writer tried to pass about Toronto.

options.A: People from different countries fight over space in the city.
options.B: People keep their different cultures but live in un-orderly manner.
options.C: People from different cultures still lead orderly life in the city.
options.D: Toronto is a good example of a melting pot, mixing of many cultures to create one culture.

explanation_steps: Each community is ‘intact, a piece in the mosaic’ (cultures kept), and ‘Toronto’s underlying orderliness was evident even here’; the city ‘has remained law-abiding’.
So cultures stay different AND life is orderly. D contradicts ‘a mosaic, not a melting pot’; A and B contradict the orderliness. Answer: C.
tips: ‘Mosaic’ = separate pieces that stay distinct; ‘melting pot’ = cultures melt into one.

similar_questions.stem: A writer says a school ‘has students from nine regions, each keeping its own songs, yet the school runs smoothly’. The message is that

options.B: different groups live together in order.

explanation_steps: Different cultures kept + runs smoothly = order. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Order in Toronto is appreciated more by the newcomers to Toronto because

options.A: the newcomers have seen what disorder can create elsewhere.
options.B: they have seen more orderly cities than Toronto.
options.C: they hope that Toronto will become more orderly.
options.D: they believe Toronto is Canada’s most orderly city.

explanation_steps: Last paragraph: newcomers ‘have seen how bad the world can get when order slips away into madness.’
That is experience of disorder elsewhere. Answer: A.
tips: Cause questions: find ‘because’ or an equivalent (‘partly because …’) in the text.

similar_questions.stem: ‘People who have lived through a drought never waste water.’ Why do they save water?

options.B: They have seen what shortage can do.

explanation_steps: Experience of hardship explains the behaviour. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Choose the best contextual meaning of the highlighted word or phrase: ‘intact’. Context: “Each community is intact, a piece in the mosaic …”
explanation_steps: ‘a piece in the mosaic’ – a mosaic piece is a single whole piece, and the text says each community stays separate and complete.
‘intact’ = whole, undamaged (in one piece). Answer: C.
tips: Replace the word with each option inside the sentence; keep the one that keeps the meaning.

similar_questions.stem: The old building survived the earthquake intact. ‘Intact’ means
explanation_steps: Survived + intact = undamaged, whole. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘intact’ in this context means ‘whole, undamaged (in one piece)’.

questions.stem: Choose the best contextual meaning of the highlighted word or phrase: ‘hectic’. Context: “Toronto’s underlying orderliness was evident even here, amid the hectic buying and selling.”
explanation_steps: ‘even here, amid the hectic buying and selling’ – ‘even’ shows a contrast with orderliness, so hectic = busy and disorderly; E is the closest option.
‘hectic’ = very busy, rushed and confused (the opposite of calm or orderly). Answer: E.
tips: Replace the word with each option inside the sentence; keep the one that keeps the meaning.

similar_questions.stem: The market was hectic on the day before the holiday. ‘Hectic’ means
explanation_steps: A market before a holiday is crowded and rushed. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘hectic’ in this context means ‘very busy, rushed and confused (the opposite of calm or orderly)’.

questions.stem: Choose the best contextual meaning of the highlighted word or phrase: ‘entrepreneur’. Context: “Ko, an entrepreneur who came to Toronto from Hong Kong in 1967 …”
explanation_steps: Ko ‘showed me the neighbourhood’ where merchants sell goods; an immigrant who built a business.
‘entrepreneur’ = a person who starts and runs a business. Answer: B.
tips: Replace the word with each option inside the sentence; keep the one that keeps the meaning.

similar_questions.stem: She became an entrepreneur when she opened her own bakery. ‘Entrepreneur’ means
explanation_steps: Opening your own business = entrepreneur. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘entrepreneur’ in this context means ‘a person who starts and runs a business’.

questions.stem: Choose the best contextual meaning of the highlighted word or phrase: ‘slips away’. Context: “… have seen how bad the world can get when order slips away into madness.”
explanation_steps: Order ‘slips away into madness’ = order disappears and chaos takes its place.
‘slips away’ = disappears gradually. Answer: A.
tips: Replace the word with each option inside the sentence; keep the one that keeps the meaning.

similar_questions.stem: As the evening went on, his confidence slipped away. ‘Slipped away’ means
explanation_steps: Confidence ‘slipping away’ = gradually disappearing. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘slips away’ in this context means ‘disappears gradually’.

questions.stem: ___11___ new health centre has been constructed at __12__ cost of five million Nakfa in our small town.
explanation_steps: The health centre is mentioned for the first time and is singular and countable → indefinite article.
‘new’ begins with a consonant sound → ‘A’, not ‘An’. ‘One’ stresses number, which is not the point. Answer: A.
tips: First mention of a singular countable noun → a/an; second mention → the.

similar_questions.stem: ___ old woman lives next door. The woman is very kind.
explanation_steps: First mention; ‘old’ starts with a vowel sound → An. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: First mention of a singular countable noun takes a/an (a before a consonant sound).

questions.stem: A new health centre has been constructed at __12__ cost of five million Nakfa in our small town.
explanation_steps: Fixed expression: ‘at a cost of + amount’.
‘cost’ begins with a consonant sound → ‘a’. Answer: B.
tips: Learn the pattern ‘at a cost of …’, ‘at a speed of …’, ‘at a price of …’.

similar_questions.stem: The bridge was built at ___ cost of two million dollars.
explanation_steps: at a cost of … Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘at a cost/price/speed of + number’ takes a.

questions.stem: __13__ health centre is going to serve the inhabitants of our town and the surrounding villages.
explanation_steps: The health centre has already been mentioned (second mention) → definite article ‘The’. Answer: B.
tips: Second mention → the.

similar_questions.stem: I bought a book yesterday. ___ book is about Eritrean history.
explanation_steps: Second mention → The. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: A noun already mentioned takes the.

questions.stem: The health centre is going to serve __14__ inhabitants of our town and the surrounding villages.
explanation_steps: ‘inhabitants’ is plural (so a/an/one are impossible) and is specified by ‘of our town and the surrounding villages’ → ‘the’. Answer: B.
tips: A noun made specific by an of-phrase takes ‘the’ (the people of Asmara).

similar_questions.stem: ___ students of our class went on a trip to Massawa.
explanation_steps: Specific group (of our class) → The. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.rule: A noun specified by an of-phrase takes the.

questions.stem: My parents and I __15__ in Massawa safely.
explanation_steps: Ruta is phoning from Massawa now: the arrival is finished and its result (they are there) matters now → present perfect.
Answer: B ‘have arrived’.
tips: Present perfect for a recent past action with a present result (we have arrived).

similar_questions.stem: Good news! We ___ the exam results.
explanation_steps: Recent action, present relevance → present perfect. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Present perfect for a recent past action with a present result (we have arrived).

questions.stem: We __16__ at the Red Sea Hotel at the moment.
explanation_steps: ‘at the moment’ → present continuous; subject ‘We’ → ‘are staying’ (A is for ‘I’).
Answer: B.
tips: ‘at the moment / now’ signals the present continuous.

similar_questions.stem: Be quiet! The baby ___ at the moment.
explanation_steps: at the moment → present continuous. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘at the moment / now’ signals the present continuous.

questions.stem: And I __17__ this public phone, and I wanted to speak to you for a while.
explanation_steps: She is using the phone now; she found it a moment ago → present perfect with ‘just’.
D (past perfect) needs another past reference point; ‘find’ is not used in the continuous here. Answer: C.
tips: ‘just’ + present perfect for an action completed a moment ago.

similar_questions.stem: Look! I ___ my lost keys under the sofa.
explanation_steps: Just completed, visible result → have just found. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘just’ + present perfect for an action completed a moment ago.

questions.stem: When __18__ back home.
explanation_steps: A question about a future time (reply: ‘On Monday morning’) → Wh-word + will + subject + base verb.
‘When will you be back home?’ A keeps statement word order; D has no subject. Answer: C.
tips: Future questions: Wh- + will + subject + verb.

similar_questions.stem: ___ the results announced?
explanation_steps: When will + subject + be … Answer: C.

textbook_ref.rule: Future questions: Wh- + will + subject + verb.

questions.stem: Next time I hope we __19__ able to go on holiday together.
explanation_steps: ‘be able to’ needs a form of ‘be’; ‘Next time’ is future → ‘will be able to’.
‘can/could/can be’ cannot be followed by ‘able’. Answer: D.
tips: Future ability = will be able to (can has no future form).

similar_questions.stem: After the course, you ___ able to speak Arabic well.
explanation_steps: Future ability → will be able to. Answer: B.

keywords: Modals – future ability (will be able to)

textbook_ref.topic: Modals – future ability (will be able to)
textbook_ref.rule: Future ability = will be able to (can has no future form).

questions.stem: Do you know where we __20__ yesterday morning?
explanation_steps: ‘yesterday morning’ = finished past time → past simple.
The present perfect (B) cannot be used with ‘yesterday’. Answer: A.
tips: Finished-time expressions (yesterday, last week, ago) take the past simple.

similar_questions.stem: We ___ to the museum last Saturday.
explanation_steps: last Saturday → past simple. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Finished-time expressions (yesterday, last week, ago) take the past simple.

questions.stem: In the afternoon we __21__ a historical place before we __22__ to Ghergusum beach.
explanation_steps: Two past actions: the visit came first, the trip to the beach second.
Earlier past action → past perfect ‘had visited’; later action → past simple ‘went’ (item 22). Answer: D.
tips: Past perfect for the earlier of two past actions (had visited … before we went).

similar_questions.stem: She ___ her homework before she watched the film.
explanation_steps: Earlier past action → past perfect. Answer: B.

keywords: Past perfect – sequence of past events

textbook_ref.topic: Past perfect – sequence of past events
textbook_ref.rule: Past perfect for the earlier of two past actions (had visited … before we went).

questions.stem: In the afternoon we had visited a historical place before we __22__ to Ghergusum beach.
explanation_steps: The later of two past actions after ‘before’ → past simple ‘went’.
‘had gone’ would make both actions ‘earlier’ and lose the sequence. Answer: E.
tips: In a ‘before/after’ clause, the later past action is in the past simple.

similar_questions.stem: They had eaten lunch before they ___ the bus.
explanation_steps: Later action → past simple. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: In a ‘before/after’ clause, the later past action is in the past simple.

questions.stem: It is a bit hot these days. But as you know I __23__ hot weather.
explanation_steps: A general fact/preference now → present simple; subject ‘I’ → ‘like’ (no -s).
Answer: B.
tips: Present simple for likes, dislikes and general truths; no -s with I/you/we/they.

similar_questions.stem: As you know, my brother ___ spicy food.
explanation_steps: Third person singular present simple → hates. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Present simple for likes, dislikes and general truths; no -s with I/you/we/they.

questions.stem: The city is the commercial centre of the country, and it is situated 3000 meters ____ sea level.
explanation_steps: Altitude is measured ‘above sea level’ (or ‘below sea level’).
Answer: B.
tips: Fixed phrase: … metres above sea level.

similar_questions.stem: The Danakil Depression lies more than 100 metres ___ sea level.
explanation_steps: A depression is lower than the sea → below sea level. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Height is given as ‘… metres above/below sea level’.

questions.stem: A: How old is your youngest daughter?  B: She was born ____ the first day of January, so she is only 6 months old now.
explanation_steps: Days and dates take ‘on’: on Monday, on 1 January, on the first day of January.
Answer: D.
tips: at + clock time; on + day/date; in + month/year/season.

similar_questions.stem: Independence Day is celebrated ___ 24 May.
explanation_steps: Date → on. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.rule: Use ‘on’ with days and dates.

questions.stem: A: Is the meeting scheduled for Tuesday?  B: Yes, but it has been put ____ for Saturday.
explanation_steps: ‘put off’ = postpone. The meeting was moved from Tuesday to a later day (Saturday).
‘put on’ (wear/stage) and the others do not fit. Answer: E.
tips: put off = postpone; call off = cancel.

similar_questions.stem: Because of the rain, the match was put ___ until next week.
explanation_steps: Postponed → put off. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: put off = postpone.

questions.stem: My mother and father are very old, and I’m the only one who ____ them.
explanation_steps: Old parents need care → ‘look after’ = take care of.
look into = investigate; take after = resemble; look for = search; look out = be careful. Answer: C.
tips: look after = take care of; take after = resemble a parent.

similar_questions.stem: Who will ___ your plants while you are away?
explanation_steps: Care for → look after. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: look after = take care of.

questions.stem: The WHO is an acronym. It ____ World Health Organization.
explanation_steps: An acronym ‘stands for’ (= represents) the full name.
stand by = support; carry on = continue; carry out = perform. Answer: A.
tips: Abbreviation X stands for Y.

similar_questions.stem: UN ___ United Nations.
explanation_steps: Abbreviation → stands for. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: stand for = represent (abbreviations).

questions.stem: The committee members discussed ____ the issues thoroughly throughout the week.
explanation_steps: ‘discuss’ is a transitive verb: discuss something (NOT ‘discuss about’).
Answer: E.
tips: discuss, enter, marry, reach, approach take a direct object – no preposition.

similar_questions.stem: We need to ___ the plan with the manager.
explanation_steps: discuss + object. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘discuss’ takes a direct object (discuss the issues).

questions.stem: Saba: The teacher will give us only half an hour to answer all of the fifty questions.  Nura: So all the questions ____ simple.
explanation_steps: Nura draws a logical conclusion: 50 questions in 30 minutes → they are surely easy.
Deduction (near certainty) about the present → ‘must be’. Answer: C.
tips: must = logical certainty (positive); can’t = logical certainty (negative); might/could = possibility.

similar_questions.stem: He has worked for twelve hours without a break. He ___ tired.
explanation_steps: Logical deduction → must be. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: must + be = logical conclusion that something is true.

questions.stem: Abel: A penalty kick was missed. Who missed it, Rezene?  Rezene: Habtom missed the penalty kick. For sure, Salim ____ it.
explanation_steps: The kick is in the past and was missed; Rezene says Salim would have been able to score it (unreal past ability).
Past possibility/ability that did not happen → could + have + past participle. The other options refer to the present/future. Answer: D.
tips: Modal + have + past participle talks about the past: could have (possible but didn’t happen), should have (advisable but didn’t happen).

similar_questions.stem: You took a taxi? You ___ walked – the shop is only 200 metres away.
explanation_steps: Past possibility not taken → could have walked. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: could have + past participle = a past possibility that did not happen.

questions.stem: Many countries of Africa ____ valuable natural resources recently.
explanation_steps: ‘recently’ signals the present perfect; subject ‘Many countries’ is plural → ‘have discovered’.
E has singular ‘has’. Answer: D.
tips: recently / lately / so far / already → present perfect.

similar_questions.stem: Scientists ___ a new species of fish recently.
explanation_steps: recently + plural subject → have found. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘recently’ takes the present perfect; the auxiliary agrees with the subject.

questions.stem: Neither onions nor garlic ____ in cooking this meal in our restaurant.
explanation_steps: With neither … nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: ‘garlic’ (uncountable, singular).
Onions and garlic do not use anything – they are used → passive ‘is used’. Answer: D.
tips: either/neither … or/nor: the verb agrees with the subject closest to it.

similar_questions.stem: Neither the students nor the teacher ___ absent today.
explanation_steps: Nearest subject ‘the teacher’ (singular) → is. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: The verb agrees with the nearer subject.

questions.stem: Zemzem would have called me if she ____ my number.
explanation_steps: Main clause ‘would have called’ = third conditional (unreal past).
If-clause of the third conditional → past perfect: ‘if she had had my number’. Answer: B.
tips: Third conditional: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle. Never ‘would’ in the if-clause.

similar_questions.stem: If we ___ earlier, we would have caught the bus.
explanation_steps: Third conditional → had left. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: If + past perfect, would have + past participle.

questions.stem: The owner and manager of the two companies ____ very happy when the technicians repaired the machine last Tuesday.
explanation_steps: Only one article: ‘The owner and manager’ = ONE person who is both owner and manager → singular verb.
Past time (last Tuesday, repaired) → ‘was’. Answer: C.
tips: ‘The owner and manager’ (one ‘the’) = one person → singular; ‘The owner and the manager’ = two people → plural.

similar_questions.stem: The poet and singer ___ arrived; everyone is waiting to hear her.
explanation_steps: One person (her) → singular ‘has’. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.topic: Subject–verb agreement – two nouns referring to one person
textbook_ref.rule: Two nouns with one article referring to the same person take a singular verb.

questions.stem: Sara: May I call you around 11:00 tomorrow?  Rahel: Yes, I ____ my exam by that time.
explanation_steps: ‘by that time’ (= by 11:00 tomorrow) → an action completed before a future moment.
That is the future perfect: ‘will have finished’. Answer: C.
tips: by + future time → future perfect (will have + past participle).

similar_questions.stem: By next June, we ___ Grade 12.
explanation_steps: by + future time → future perfect. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: by + future time → will have + past participle.

questions.stem: Rahwa is a great footballer; ____, she is a successful business woman.
explanation_steps: The second clause ADDS another positive fact → additive connector ‘moreover’.
however = contrast; therefore = result; although / in spite of cannot follow a semicolon + comma pattern like this. Answer: B.
tips: ; moreover, / ; however, / ; therefore, — the sentence connector shows the relationship (addition, contrast, result).

similar_questions.stem: The hotel is cheap; ___, it is very close to the beach.
explanation_steps: Adding another advantage → moreover. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.rule: moreover / furthermore / in addition add a similar idea.

questions.stem: Only two students understood the instruction, ____?
explanation_steps: The verb is past simple (understood) → the tag uses ‘did’ (B, C are present; D is not a tag).
‘Only two students’ means ‘very few students’ – a restrictive/semi-negative subject, like ‘few’ or ‘hardly anyone’. A negative-meaning statement takes a positive tag → ‘did they?’.
Some grammars accept ‘didn’t they?’ after ‘only’, but the item is clearly built to test the semi-negative rule. Answer: E.
tips: Semi-negative words (few, little, hardly, seldom, only + number) usually take a POSITIVE tag.

similar_questions.stem: Few people came to the meeting, ___?
explanation_steps: ‘Few’ is negative in meaning → positive tag. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Statements with few/little/hardly/only (restrictive meaning) take a positive tag.

questions.review_flag: Teacher decision: tags after ‘only + number’ are disputed in grammar references. Keyed E ‘did they’ (semi-negative ‘only two’ = few → positive tag); A ‘didn’t they’ is the answer some teachers accept for a positive statement.

questions.stem: You can’t smoke here. It’s ____.
explanation_steps: ‘You can’t smoke’ → smoking is forbidden = prohibited.
allowed / permitted / approved mean the opposite. Answer: E.
tips: prohibited = forbidden (by law or a rule).

similar_questions.stem: You mustn’t use your phone in the exam hall. Phones are ___.
explanation_steps: mustn’t → banned. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: prohibited = not allowed.

questions.stem: Henok: I don’t do well in my exams.  Ali: You have to avoid ____ silly mistakes first.
explanation_steps: ‘avoid’ is followed by a gerund (-ing): avoid making.
Answer: C.
tips: Verbs + -ing: avoid, enjoy, finish, mind, deny, suggest, keep, practise.

similar_questions.stem: You should avoid ___ too much sugar.
explanation_steps: avoid + -ing. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.rule: avoid + -ing.

questions.stem: Both alternatives are not good, but you must choose the ____ evil.
explanation_steps: Idiom: ‘the lesser of two evils / the lesser evil’ – comparing TWO things, so a comparative is needed.
‘lesser’ is the comparative adjective used before a noun (less is used with uncountable quantities). Answer: A.
tips: the lesser evil = the less harmful of two bad choices.

similar_questions.stem: Of the two injuries, the broken finger was the ___ problem.
explanation_steps: Two things compared, before a noun → lesser. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: lesser (comparative of little, used before a noun): the lesser evil.

questions.stem: Students should not waste their precious time unnecessarily. ____
explanation_steps: Negative statement → negative addition: ‘Teachers shouldn’t either’ or ‘Neither should teachers’.
B and C use a double negative; D and E are for positive statements. Answer: A.
tips: Negative additions: …n’t either / Neither (Nor) + auxiliary + subject (no ‘not’ after neither).

similar_questions.stem: I can’t swim. ___
explanation_steps: Negative → can’t either. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Negative statement → …n’t either / Neither + aux + subject.

questions.stem: Hirut and Zahra scored the highest mark in their class. ____
explanation_steps: Positive statement in the past simple (scored) → So + did + subject.
Answer: D ‘So did I’.
tips: Additions copy the auxiliary: past simple → did; present simple → do/does; be → am/is/are/was/were.

similar_questions.stem: My brother finished the race. ___
explanation_steps: Past simple → So did I. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Positive statement → So + auxiliary + subject.

questions.stem: Choose the clause which is connected correctly.

options.A: Because he’d never tried it before, he was very good at it.
options.B: Despite he’d never tried it before, he was very good at it.
options.C: In spite of he’d never tried it before, he was very good at it.
options.D: Since he’d never tried it before, he was very good at it.
options.E: Although he’d never tried it before, he was very good at it.

explanation_steps: Never having tried something and still being very good at it is a CONTRAST.
Because/Since (A, D) give a reason – illogical. Despite/In spite of (B, C) must be followed by a noun or -ing, not a full clause.
‘Although + clause’ is correct. Answer: E.
tips: Despite/in spite of + noun/-ing (Despite never having tried it …); although + subject + verb.

similar_questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: Despite it was raining, we went out.
options.B: Although it was raining, we went out.
options.C: Because it was raining, we went out.
options.D: In spite of it was raining, we went out.
options.E: Since it was raining, we went out.

explanation_steps: Contrast + full clause → although. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: although + clause; despite/in spite of + noun/-ing; in addition to + -ing (adding); because/since = reason.

questions.stem: Choose the clause which is connected correctly.

options.A: Despite being an accomplished musician, Muna is also a great painter.
options.B: Since being an accomplished musician, Muna is also a great painter.
options.C: In addition to being an accomplished musician, Muna is also a great painter.
options.D: Though being an accomplished musician, Muna is also a great painter.
options.E: As being an accomplished musician, Muna is also a great painter.

explanation_steps: ‘also’ shows the second fact is ADDED to the first (two talents), not contrasted.
‘In addition to + -ing’ is the additive pattern. Despite/Though = contrast; Since/As = reason, and ‘as being’ is ungrammatical. Answer: C.
tips: The word ‘also’ in the main clause is a clue for ‘in addition to / besides’.

similar_questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: Despite speaking Tigrinya, he also speaks Arabic.
options.B: Besides speaking Tigrinya, he also speaks Arabic.
options.C: Since speaking Tigrinya, he also speaks Arabic.
options.D: Although speaking Tigrinya, he also speaks Arabic.
options.E: As speaking Tigrinya, he also speaks Arabic.

explanation_steps: Addition + also → Besides + -ing. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: although + clause; despite/in spite of + noun/-ing; in addition to + -ing (adding); because/since = reason.

questions.stem: Choose the inverted form of the given sentence: This bank not only provides the best service, but it also pays the highest interest rate.

options.A: Not only does this bank provides the best service, but it also pays the highest interest rate.
options.B: Not only this bank provides the best service, but it also pays the highest interest rate.
options.C: Not only does this bank provide the best service, but it also pays the highest interest rate.
options.D: Not only is this bank providing the best service, but it also pays the highest interest rate.
options.E: Not only did this bank provide the best service, but it also pays the highest interest rate.

explanation_steps: Fronted ‘Not only’ → question word order. Present simple ‘provides’ → does + subject + base verb.
A keeps the -s after ‘does’; B has no inversion; D changes to continuous; E changes to past. Answer: C.
tips: After do/does/did the main verb is always the base form (does … provide).

similar_questions.stem: Choose the inverted form: She not only sings well but also dances beautifully.

options.B: Not only does she sings well …
options.C: Not only does she sing well, but she also dances beautifully.
options.D: Not only did she sing well …
options.E: Not only is she singing well …

explanation_steps: does + subject + base verb, same tense. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.rule: Not only + auxiliary + subject + base verb; keep the tense.

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect speech form: “When are we going to submit the group assignment?” the students said to the teacher.

options.A: The students asked the teacher if they were going to submit the group assignment?
options.B: The students asked the teacher if they were going to submit the group assignment.
options.C: The students asked the teacher when they were going to submit the group assignment.
options.D: The students asked the teacher whether they are going to submit the group assignment.
options.E: The students asked the teacher whether they are going to submit the group assignment?

explanation_steps: A wh-question keeps its wh-word (‘when’); if/whether is only for yes/no questions → A, B, D, E are wrong.
Tense shifts back (are → were), statement word order, full stop. Answer: C.
tips: Reported questions never end with a question mark.

similar_questions.stem: “Where do you live?” he asked me.

options.A: He asked me where did I live.
options.B: He asked me where I lived.
options.C: He asked me if I lived.
options.D: He asked me where I lived?
options.E: He asked me whether I live.

explanation_steps: wh-word + statement order + backshift. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Wh-questions are reported with the wh-word + statement order; yes/no questions with if/whether; tenses shift back; no question mark.

questions.stem: Choose the correct direct speech form: The woman warned her son not to press the red button under any circumstances.

options.A: The woman said to her son do not press this button under any circumstances.
options.B: The woman said to her son,,do not press this button under any circumstances.
options.C: The woman said to her son, “do not press this button under any circumstances.”
options.D: The woman said to her son, “Do not press this button under any circumstances.”
options.E: The woman, “said to her son do not press this button under any circumstances.”

explanation_steps: Direct speech needs: a comma after the reporting clause, opening and closing quotation marks around the exact words, and a CAPITAL letter at the start of the quotation.
C lacks the capital ‘Do’; A, B have no quotation marks; E puts them in the wrong place. Answer: D.
tips: Direct speech: Reporting clause + comma + “Capital … .”

similar_questions.stem: Choose the correct direct speech: The teacher told us to open our books.

options.A: The teacher said to us, “open your books.”
options.B: The teacher said to us, “Open your books.”
options.C: The teacher said to us “Open your books”
options.D: The teacher, “said to us open your books.”
options.E: The teacher said to us open your books.

explanation_steps: Comma, quotation marks, capital letter. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Comma + opening quotation mark + capital letter; closing punctuation inside the quotation marks.

questions.review_flag: The indirect sentence says ‘the red button’ but every option says ‘this button’ – a small inconsistency in the paper; it does not affect the answer.

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect speech form: The teacher said to the student, “Do you revise your lessons at home?”

options.A: The teacher asked the student if she revised her lessons at home.
options.B: The teacher asked the student if she had revised her lessons at home.
options.C: The teacher asked the student if did she revise her lessons at home?
options.D: The teacher asked the student if she revises her lessons at home.
options.E: The teacher asked the student if she has revised her lessons at home?

explanation_steps: Yes/no question → ‘if/whether’ + statement word order.
Past reporting verb → present simple shifts to past simple: revise → revised.

B shifts two steps (past perfect); C keeps question order; D does not backshift (possible only if the habit is still true, but the standard answer is the backshifted form); E has the wrong tense and a question mark. Answer: A.
tips: Backshift: present simple → past simple; present perfect → past perfect.

similar_questions.stem: She said to me, “Do you like tea?”

options.A: She asked me if I liked tea.
options.B: She asked me if did I like tea.
options.C: She asked me if I had liked tea.
options.D: She asked me do I like tea.
options.E: She asked me if I like tea?

explanation_steps: if + statement order + backshift. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: Wh-questions are reported with the wh-word + statement order; yes/no questions with if/whether; tenses shift back; no question mark.

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive form: Why did the director collect all of our documents?

options.A: Why were all of our documents collected by the director?
options.B: Why were all of our documents collected by the director.
options.C: Why have all of our documents collected by the director?
options.D: Why did all of our documents collected by the director?
options.E: Why are all of our documents collected by the director.

explanation_steps: Past simple active question (did … collect) → past simple passive question: Why + were + subject + past participle?
B lacks the question mark; C, E change the tense (and C lacks ‘been’); D uses ‘did’ with a past participle. Answer: A.
tips: Passive past simple = was/were + past participle.

similar_questions.stem: Passive of: When did they build the bridge?
explanation_steps: Past simple question → was + subject + built? Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: Keep the tense; object → subject; be + past participle; keep question order and punctuation.

questions.stem: Choose the correct active form: The patients were being treated regularly by the doctor.

options.A: The doctor was treated the patients regularly.
options.B: The doctor has treated the patients regularly.
options.C: The doctor is treating the patients regularly.
options.D: The doctor treated the patients regularly.
options.E: The doctor was treating the patients regularly.

explanation_steps: ‘were being treated’ = past continuous passive.
Active past continuous with singular subject ‘the doctor’ → ‘was treating’. Answer: E.
tips: being + past participle = continuous passive.

similar_questions.stem: Active of: The road was being repaired by the workers.

options.B: The workers were repairing the road.
options.C: The workers are repairing the road.
options.D: The workers have repaired the road.
options.E: The workers was repairing the road.

explanation_steps: Past continuous, plural subject → were repairing. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Keep the tense; object → subject; be + past participle; keep question order and punctuation.

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive form: Our chemistry teacher has used all of the chemicals in the laboratory this academic year.

options.A: All of the chemicals in the laboratory has been used by our chemistry teacher this academic year.
options.B: All of the chemicals in the laboratory were being used by our chemistry teacher this academic year.
options.C: All of the chemicals in the laboratory have been used by our chemistry teacher this academic year.
options.D: All of the chemicals in the laboratory would have been used by our chemistry teacher this academic year.
options.E: All of the chemicals in the laboratory had been used by our chemistry teacher that academic year.

explanation_steps: Present perfect active (has used) → present perfect passive (have/has been used).
The new subject ‘All of the chemicals’ is plural → ‘have been used’ (A has singular ‘has’). Answer: C.
tips: In the passive, the verb agrees with the NEW subject.

similar_questions.stem: Passive of: The students have planted many trees.

options.A: Many trees has been planted by the students.
options.B: Many trees have been planted by the students.
options.C: Many trees were planted by the students.
options.D: Many trees had been planted by the students.
options.E: Many trees have planted by the students.

explanation_steps: Present perfect passive, plural subject → have been planted. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Keep the tense; object → subject; be + past participle; keep question order and punctuation.

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the given sentence: I’ll lend her the money as long as she pays me back.

options.A: I’ll lend her for a long time.
options.B: I’ll lend her only if she pays me back.
options.C: I’ll lend her only if she pays me back after a long time.
options.D: I won’t lend her for a short time.
options.E: I won’t lend her for a long time.

explanation_steps: ‘as long as’ here is a conjunction of condition = ‘only if / provided that’, not a time expression.
Answer: B.
tips: as long as / provided that / on condition that = only if.

similar_questions.stem: You can borrow my bike as long as you return it tonight.

options.A: You can keep the bike for a long time.
options.B: You can borrow it only if you return it tonight.
options.E: You can borrow it after tonight.

explanation_steps: as long as = only if. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Choose the option with the same meaning – no more, no less.

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the given sentence: Elsa and Abel are teaching English and mathematics, respectively in Warsay Yikealo Secondary School.

options.A: Abel is teaching mathematic and Elsa is teaching English.
options.B: Elsa is teaching mathematics and Abel is teaching English.
options.C: Elsa and Abel are teaching both subjects.
options.D: Elsa and Abel are respected teachers in Warsay Yikaalo.
options.E: Abel and Elsa respect the teaching profession.

explanation_steps: ‘respectively’ pairs the lists in order: Elsa → English, Abel → mathematics.
A says exactly this (in reverse order of names). ‘respectively’ has nothing to do with respect (D, E). Answer: A.
tips: respectively = in the same order as the items mentioned.

similar_questions.stem: Semhar and Yonas came first and second, respectively.

options.B: Semhar came first and Yonas second.

explanation_steps: Order is kept. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Choose the option with the same meaning – no more, no less.

questions.review_flag: Option A has the typo ‘mathematic’ (for mathematics); it is still the only correct paraphrase.

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the given sentence: Dogs are intelligent but not as intelligent as chimpanzees.

options.A: Dogs are less intelligent than many animals.
options.C: Chimpanzees are less intelligent than dogs.
options.D: Chimpanzees are more intelligent than dogs.
options.E: Both dogs and chimpanzees are more intelligent than most animals.

explanation_steps: ‘not as … as chimpanzees’ → chimpanzees have more intelligence than dogs.
A, B, E add information that is not in the sentence; C reverses it. Answer: D.
tips: X is not as big as Y = Y is bigger than X.

similar_questions.stem: Keren is not as hot as Massawa.
explanation_steps: not as … as → the second is more. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Choose the option with the same meaning – no more, no less.

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the given dialogue: Robel: Are you going to give all of this food to the dogs?  Meron: Yes, I love the dogs very much.

options.E: Meron and Robel love dogs very much.

explanation_steps: ‘the dogs’ with the definite article = specific dogs known to both speakers (the ones getting the food).
‘dogs’ without ‘the’ would mean dogs in general (A, D). Nothing is said about Robel’s feelings. Answer: C.
tips: Zero article + plural = things in general; ‘the’ + plural = specific ones.

similar_questions.stem: ‘I like the flowers in your garden.’ This means the speaker likes
explanation_steps: the + plural = specific. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Plural nouns without ‘the’ refer to things in general; with ‘the’ they refer to specific ones.

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the given sentence: I wish I had bought the computer.

options.A: I had a plan to buy a computer.
options.B: I bought a cell phone instead of a computer.
options.D: I didn’t have enough money to buy a computer.

explanation_steps: wish + past perfect expresses regret about the past: the speaker did NOT buy the computer.
The reason (money, a phone) is not stated. Answer: C.
tips: wish + had + past participle → the opposite happened in the past.

similar_questions.stem: I wish I had studied harder.
explanation_steps: Regret → I didn’t study hard. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: wish + past perfect = regret about the past (the opposite is true).

questions.stem: Through out history, women have had responsibility for healing the __58__.
explanation_steps: You heal people who are ill: ‘the sick’ (the + adjective = a group of people).
Answer: C.
tips: the sick / the poor / the elderly = groups of people.

similar_questions.stem: Nurses spend their lives caring for the ___.
explanation_steps: Caring (medically) → the sick. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: heal the sick (the + adjective as a plural noun).

questions.stem: However, it is only in recent times that they have been __59__ to train as doctors at medical schools in many countries.
explanation_steps: ‘However … only in recent times’ contrasts with ‘they have made an enormous contribution in that short time’ → they have only recently been permitted to train.
‘be allowed to + verb’ fits; refused/stopped/deprived have the opposite meaning or wrong pattern. Answer: B.
tips: be allowed to do = be permitted to do.

similar_questions.stem: Only since 1990 have girls in that village been ___ to attend secondary school.
explanation_steps: Only recently permitted → allowed. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: be allowed to + verb = be permitted.

questions.stem: Yet in that short time, they have made an enormous __60__ to modern medicine.
explanation_steps: Collocation: make a contribution to something.
participation is ‘in’, not ‘to’, and does not collocate with ‘make’. Answer: A.
tips: make a contribution to = help to achieve or improve.

similar_questions.stem: Farmers make an important ___ to the national economy.
explanation_steps: make a contribution to. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: make a contribution to (collocation).

questions.stem: Student: Excuse me, teacher. I’m going to miss tomorrow’s classes.  Teacher: ____61____?  Student: Yes, it is.

options.D: Would you tell me the reason?
options.E: Do you want to miss classes?

explanation_steps: The reply ‘Yes, it is.’ needs a yes/no question with ‘Is it …?’.
Only B fits (C would be answered ‘No, I’m not’; A and D are not yes/no questions). Later ‘It is really important’ confirms. Answer: B.
tips: Short answers repeat the auxiliary of the question: Is it …? – Yes, it is.

similar_questions.stem: A: ___?  B: Yes, it is. It starts at eight.
explanation_steps: Yes, it is ← Is …? Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Use the next line: the reply shows the form and topic of the missing line.

questions.stem: Teacher: ____62____  Student: I’ve made arrangements with my seatmate. …, I’m going to do a lot of extra reading.

options.A: Where do you want to go?
options.B: Will you miss only tomorrow’s classes?
options.E: How are you going to catch up?

explanation_steps: The student answers with her plan for the missed lessons (arrangements with a seatmate, extra reading).
That answers ‘How are you going to catch up?’. Answer: E.
tips: Read the answer first, then choose the question it responds to.

similar_questions.stem: A: ___  B: I’ll take the early bus and study on the way.
explanation_steps: The reply is a plan → How will you manage? Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: Use the next line: the reply shows the form and topic of the missing line.

questions.stem: Student: I’ve made arrangements with my seatmate. ___63___, I’m going to do a lot of extra reading.
explanation_steps: Extra reading is a second way of catching up, added to the first → ‘In addition’.
Although/Despite/In contrast show contrast; For instance gives an example. Answer: D.
tips: Sentence-initial connectors: In addition (add), However/In contrast (contrast), For instance (example).

similar_questions.stem: I will attend the extra classes. ___, I will ask my brother for help.
explanation_steps: Adding → In addition. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: In addition, … adds another point.

questions.stem: Teacher: You know that I only allow one absence per semester, ___64___?
explanation_steps: The main clause is ‘You know …’ (positive, present simple) → negative tag with do: ‘don’t you?’.
Answer: C.
tips: Positive statement → negative tag; present simple lexical verb → do/does.

similar_questions.stem: You live near the school, ___?
explanation_steps: Positive present simple → don’t you. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: Positive statement + negative tag; the tag uses the auxiliary of the main clause (do for present simple).

questions.stem: Teacher: Well, use your day off effectively.  Student: ___65___. Thank you, teacher.
explanation_steps: The teacher gives advice; the natural reply is a promise to follow it: ‘I’ll do so.’
The other options are questions and do not fit before ‘Thank you’. Answer: C.
tips: Reply to advice: I will. / I’ll do so. / I’ll try.

similar_questions.stem: A: Drive carefully.  B: ___. See you tomorrow.
explanation_steps: Promise to follow advice. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Use the next line: the reply shows the form and topic of the missing line.

questions.stem: In the first paragraph, the writer stated: “The good news is that present levels of inequality are not inevitable.” What is the point the writer makes in this sentence?

options.A: Inequality is to stay with us for a long period to come.
options.B: Inequality is a natural thing and we should accept it.
options.C: Inequality can be reduced from present levels.
options.D: High levels of inequality are unavoidable.

explanation_steps: ‘not inevitable’ = not unavoidable; the next sentence: ‘There are concrete steps governments can take to tackle inequality.’
So inequality can be reduced. A, B, D say the opposite. Answer: C.
tips: Answer from the text only; check every option in ‘A and B’ / ‘NOT’ questions.

similar_questions.stem: ‘Traffic accidents are not inevitable; most can be prevented by careful driving.’ The point is that accidents
explanation_steps: not inevitable = avoidable. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Most technological advancements are the results of decisions made by
explanation_steps: Paragraph 3: ‘the product of decisions made by research managers, businesspeople, investors, governments, and consumers.’
All the groups in A–D are listed. Answer: E.
tips: Answer from the text only; check every option in ‘A and B’ / ‘NOT’ questions.

similar_questions.stem: ‘The festival was organised by teachers, parents and students.’ Who organised it?
explanation_steps: All three are listed. Answer: E.

questions.stem: Which one of the following does the writer blame for high levels of inequality?

options.A: Increases in income by people at the top of the income distribution.
options.B: Increases in levels of poverty among those at the bottom of the income distribution.
options.C: The lack of support to the poor from the rich.

questions.stem:
PART II: PARAGRAPH WRITING. Write a meaningful and grammatically correct paragraph of about 200 words on ONE of the topics provided. You are advised to spend ONE HOUR writing your paragraph. During this time, you should prepare an outline, write and make any necessary changes to your paragraph. Your paragraph will be graded on Content, Language, and Organization.
Topics to choose from:
1. Write about your favourite animal. Compare it to the animal you like least or do not like.
2. Compare living in a village with living in a city.
questions.answer:
Write ONE paragraph on ONE topic.

Model paragraph for Topic 1 (202 words):
My favourite animal is the camel, while the animal I like least is the hyena, and the two could hardly be more different. First of all, the camel is one of the most useful animals in Eritrea. It carries heavy loads across the hot lowlands and the desert for days without drinking water, and it gives people milk, meat and leather. The hyena, on the other hand, is useless to people; it lives by hunting weak animals and eating the remains of dead ones. Secondly, the two animals differ in their behaviour. The camel is calm, patient and obedient, so even a child can lead a whole caravan. In contrast, the hyena is noisy and aggressive, and its frightening laugh at night makes villagers worry about their goats and sheep. In addition, the camel is a symbol of endurance for us Eritreans, whereas the hyena appears in many of our folk stories as a greedy and foolish creature. Finally, a camel is a valuable possession that can support a whole family, but a hyena brings only loss to farmers. In conclusion, I admire the camel for its strength, patience and usefulness, while I dislike the hyena because it is dangerous and harmful.

Model paragraph for Topic 2 (207 words):
Living in a village and living in a city are different in many ways, and each has its own advantages. To begin with, life in a village is quiet and peaceful. The air is clean, there is little traffic, and people wake up to the sound of birds rather than cars. In a city, by contrast, life is busy and noisy, and the streets are crowded with people and vehicles. Secondly, social relationships differ. Villagers know one another well and help each other in farming, weddings and times of trouble, whereas city dwellers are often too busy to know even their neighbours. However, the city offers far more services and opportunities. It has better schools, colleges, hospitals, electricity, clean water and a wide range of jobs, while many villages still lack these facilities, so young people often have to travel long distances to study or find work. Moreover, the cost of living is usually lower in a village, because people grow much of their own food, but in a city almost everything must be bought. In conclusion, village life is calmer, cheaper and closer to nature, while city life is more convenient and full of opportunities, so the better choice depends on what a person values most.

explanation_steps: Choose ONE topic. Both are comparison–contrast topics: the paragraph must compare two things, not describe only one.
Plan: topic sentence naming both things → 3–4 points of comparison (point-by-point: each supporting sentence compares both sides) → concluding sentence.
Use comparison/contrast language: whereas, while, in contrast, on the other hand, however, both … and, more … than, as … as.
Keep to about 200 words, one paragraph, and check grammar, spelling and punctuation at the end.
marking_points: Content (8): relevant topic sentence and 3–4 developed supporting points; comparison topics must compare (similarities and differences), not just describe.
Organization (6): topic sentence, logically ordered supporting sentences with transitions, a concluding sentence; ONE paragraph; unity (no irrelevant sentences).
Language (6): grammar (tenses, agreement, articles, comparatives), vocabulary, spelling and punctuation.
Length: about 200 words; clearly shorter paragraphs lose content marks.

descriptors: 7–8: clear topic sentence; 3–4 well-developed, relevant supporting points with examples or explanations; for comparison topics real similarities AND differences; about 200 words.
5–6: relevant with some support, but one point is thin or repeated.
3–4: few ideas, little support, partly off topic, or clearly too short (under about 120 words).
5–6: topic sentence → ordered supporting sentences → concluding sentence; one main idea only; smooth transitions (first of all, moreover, however, whereas, in conclusion).
3–4: logical overall, but weak or missing concluding sentence, few or repeated linkers, or one sentence off the main idea.
1–2: ideas in random order; no clear topic sentence; written as a list or several paragraphs.
5–6: accurate tenses, agreement and articles; varied sentence types; suitable vocabulary (comparatives and contrast words for comparison topics); correct spelling, capitals and punctuation.
3–4: several errors that do not block meaning; limited sentence variety or vocabulary.
1–2: frequent errors that sometimes block meaning.
0: errors make the paragraph impossible to follow.

similar_questions.stem: Write a paragraph of about 200 words comparing studying alone with studying in a group.
similar_questions.answer: Model: Studying alone and studying in a group both help students prepare for exams, but they suit different needs. First, studying alone allows a student to concentrate fully and to work at his or her own speed, whereas a group often moves too fast for some members and too slowly for others. Secondly, a group offers help that a single student cannot get. When one member does not understand a lesson, another can explain it, while a student working alone may stay confused for hours. However, groups can easily waste time, because friends start chatting about unrelated topics; in contrast, a student alone has fewer distractions. In addition, discussing questions aloud in a group improves understanding and memory, while silent reading alone is better for memorising facts and formulas. Finally, studying alone requires strong self-discipline, but a group encourages members to keep a regular timetable. In conclusion, both methods are useful, so the best plan is to study alone most of the time and to meet a small, serious group before exams.
explanation_steps: Topic sentence names both methods and says they differ.
Each supporting sentence compares both sides using whereas / while / in contrast / however.
The concluding sentence gives a balanced judgement.
